definition.name: claim_router
definition.description: Route a claim to the check that suits how it was reasoned (Peirce: deduction, induction, abduction), using all four TypeSafe patterns: one fan-out stage asks every question at once; composites weight the warning signs; confidence gates send unclear cases to a second opinion; routes name the next check for the host to run. item = {claim, basis, action?} where action is what will be done if the claim is believed. The server only labels; the host runs the check. Judges wording and stated basis, not truth.
definition.notes: v1, 2026-09-22. Built from inference_warrant v3 questions (verbatim) plus a stakes score. Findings carried over: overclaim fires on most flat statements, so it is weighted and not a route by itself; absence_as_evidence was the cleanest signal, so it routes directly; rivals cannot be judged without supplied candidates, so abduction routes to test_rivals (host lists rivals, evidence_stance judges them). Thresholds (0.6, 0.45, 0.35, 0.8) are authored guesses to be evaluated.

mode.instructions: How does item.claim relate to item.basis? Judge the logical relationship, not the topic or the confidence words.

criteria.deduction: item.basis states a general rule plus a specific case, and item.claim is exactly what that rule implies for that case. The claim would be necessarily true if the basis is true.
criteria.induction: item.basis reports observed instances, counts, tests, or measurements, and item.claim generalizes them into a pattern, rule, or prediction about cases not observed.
criteria.abduction: item.basis reports an observation or symptom, and item.claim proposes a cause, explanation, or hidden state that would account for it.
criteria.recommendation: item.claim says what should be done, decided, or how something should be read or treated, rather than stating what is true.
criteria.unsupported: item.basis is empty, says '(none)', or gives no reason that actually connects to item.claim.

certainty.instructions: How much certainty does the wording of item.claim itself express? Look only at item.claim's own words.
criteria: Explicitly tentative: might, possibly, one hypothesis, a guess
Probable: probably, likely, suggests, plausibly, most likely
Stated as plain fact with no hedge
Absolute: always, never, certainly, proves, impossible, nothing else could

overclaim.instructions: Is item.claim worded with more certainty than item.basis can license? Rules: a strict derivation from a stated general rule and case may be stated as certain. A generalization from observed instances may be stated at most as probable, and less so the fewer the instances. A proposed explanation of an observation may be stated at most as plausible, never as the only possibility. A recommendation is fine if item.basis gives a reason for it. A claim with no connecting reason may not be stated as fact at all.

criteria.true: item.claim asserts as fact, certainty, 'always', or 'the only explanation' something that item.basis only makes probable, plausible, or does not support.
criteria.false: item.claim's wording is at or below the confidence that item.basis supports, or it is a recommendation that item.basis gives a reason for.

scope_gap.instructions: Is item.claim about a broader or different subject than the thing item.basis actually measured or observed? Example: the basis measured one component, one tool, one channel, one machine, or one sample, while the claim speaks about a whole system, all users, or a different component. Compare the subject of item.claim with the subject of item.basis word by word.

criteria.true: The subject of item.claim is wider than, or different from, what item.basis measured or observed.
criteria.false: item.claim is about the same thing item.basis measured or observed.

absence_as_evidence.instructions: Does item.basis support item.claim mainly by not having seen, noticed, or found something, without describing a search thorough enough that it would have found it if it existed?

criteria.true: item.basis rests on 'I have not seen / did not notice / am not aware of' something, with no systematic search described.
criteria.false: item.basis reports positive observations, or describes a search that would have found the thing if it existed.

stakes.instructions: If item.claim were false and someone went ahead with item.action (or relied on item.claim, if no action is given), how bad would the result be?
criteria: Low: harmless or trivially undone, such as a wording choice or a log message
Medium: wasted time, rework, or a confusing result that someone would notice and fix
High: lost data, money, security, safety, or trust, or something hard to undo such as removing a safeguard or shipping to production

warrant_risk.description: How far the wording outruns the stated basis, weighted toward the clearest signals.

priority.description: What to check first: warning signs plus stakes.

routes.description: No reason given. Ask for or find the basis before anything else.
Rests on not having seen something. Run a search that would find it (docs, web, repo) before asserting.
Jev cannot tell what kind of reasoning this is. Have another judge or a person classify it.
Wording fits the basis and little is at stake. No further check.
Deduction: check the derivation with a prover (mcp-logic prove, efh-core verify_implication) or by re-deriving it.
Induction: check sample size, representativeness, and whether the claim is hedged to match.
Abduction: list rival explanations, then run evidence_stance with them as items and the observations in context.
Recommendation: check that the stated reasons actually support the action and its stakes.
